title: MUSE: Multi-Level Memory with Selective Runtime Injection for Scientific Coding Agents
summary: MUSE replaces single-level task retrieval for coding agents with a three-tier memory (global, approach-level, implementation-level) plus an LLM gate that decides whether to inject implementation experience during execution. It costs an offline memory-construction pipeline over historical trajectories, additional retrieval and gate LLM calls at runtime (extra latency and API spend), and ongoing memory curation complexity. It can fail if historical trajectories are scarce or unrepresentative, if the gate injects irrelevant advice that distracts the agent, or if benchmarks-style scientific coding does not match the reader's actual workloads.
rationale: The approach is implementable with a single GPU or API-only setup and claims quality gains on coding-agent tasks, but the benefit depends on having suitable historical trajectories and must be validated on the reader's own workload before production adoption.
technique: Multi-level agent memory with gated runtime injection

claims.statement: MUSE replaces single-level task retrieval for coding agents with a three-tier memory (global, approach-level, implementation-level) plus an LLM gate that decides whether to inject implementation experience during execution. It costs an offline memory-construction pipeline over historical trajectories, additional retrieval and gate LLM calls at runtime (extra latency and API spend), and ongoing memory curation complexity. It can fail if historical trajectories are scarce or unrepresentative, if the gate injects irrelevant advice that distracts the agent, or if benchmarks-style scientific coding does not match the reader's actual workloads.

MUSE outperforms retrieval and memory baselines on all evaluation metrics across four benchmarks spanning numerical problem solving, kernel optimization, and scientific software repair; no specific numerical improvement is stated in the abstract.
